betterCitation: Emily Dickinson, ‘We never know how high we are’, Poems, Third Series, ed. Mabel Loomis Todd, Life XIV (Roberts Brothers, 1896)
reason:
The citation is true to the edition it names and I could not fault a word of it. I refute on what the card does not say, which in a Dickinson card is the whole game, and on the fact that this file has already shipped two Dickinson cards that handle the same problem the other way.

WHAT I READ. Project Gutenberg 12242, Poems by Emily Dickinson, Three Series, Complete, downloaded and read this run. After Todd's preface signed ‘M. L. T.’ and dated ‘AMHERST, October, 1896’ the Third Series opens ‘I. LIFE.’ and runs I. REAL RICHES, II. SUPERIORITY TO FATE, III. HOPE, and so on to XIV. ASPIRATION:

  We never know how high we are
    Till we are called to rise;
  And then, if we are true to plan,
    Our statures touch the skies.

  The heroism we recite
    Would be a daily thing,
  Did not ourselves the cubits warp
    For fear to be a king.

So every element of the proposed citation checks: Third Series, Part I Life, poem XIV, titled ASPIRATION, lines 1 to 4 of 8, ‘called to rise’, semicolon at the end of line 2, full stop at the end of line 4, Roberts Brothers 1896, Todd as editor. The wording on the card exists in the named edition exactly. shipped.js: shipped [], near [], emily dickinson at 2 of 3, months [1, 2], not banned, so there is one slot left and this would take it.

GROUND ONE: THE CARD SHIPS AN EDITORIAL TEXT IN SILENCE, AND THE NOTE IS EMPTY. Todd and Higginson did not print Dickinson; they smoothed her. The proof is inside the very poem quoted: the 1896 text's second stanza reads ‘Would be a daily thing’ and ‘For fear to be a king’, where the manuscript text printed since Johnson's edition of 1955 reads ‘Would be a normal thing’ and ‘For fear to be a King’. The first stanza carries the same kind of change, and it falls on the card's own second line: the received text is ‘Till we are asked to rise’, not ‘called to rise’, with the dash at the end of the stanza and no title at all, since ‘Aspiration’ is Todd's invention and Dickinson titled almost nothing. I did not get a Johnson or Franklin edition open this run, and I say that plainly, because both are in copyright and neither is on Wikisource, whose only two versions of this poem are the 1896 Third Series and the 1924 Complete Poems, and the 1924 volume is Todd-derived too. So I assert the ‘daily / normal’ and ‘king / King’ divergence as read, and the ‘called / asked’ divergence as the reading I know to be the received one and would have the lander confirm against a Johnson or Franklin before it goes out. What is certain either way is that the title is editorial and the text is the 1896 editors' text, and the note says none of it. The note field is an empty string.

GROUND TWO: IT BREAKS THE FILE'S OWN DICKINSON PRACTICE, AND THAT PRACTICE EXISTS FOR THIS EXACT REASON. The two Dickinson cards already landed both identify the poem by first line and by number, never by an 1896 title: ‘Emily Dickinson, ‘A word is dead’ (Franklin 278), Poems, Third Series, ed. Mabel Loomis Todd, Life VI (1896)’ and ‘Emily Dickinson, ‘If I can stop one heart from breaking’ (Fr982, J919), Poems, ed. Todd and Higginson (Roberts Brothers, 1890), Life VI’. Both also carry the Life section number. This card does neither: it prints ‘Aspiration’ as though it were the poem's name, and it drops the section. A reader holding the year's three Dickinson cards side by side sees two anchored to the modern numbering and one floating under a Victorian editor's title. That inconsistency is not cosmetic here, because adding the number the house style wants is precisely what would expose the variant: put ‘(Fr1197, J1176)’ on this card and the source line would point a reader at a text that does not read ‘called’.

WHAT PASSES. Attribution is Dickinson's beyond dispute and nothing on the misattribution list touches her. No speaker is owed. Scope: verse, 1896, not scripture, not film, not lyric, not proverb, not business, not oratory. Publishable: nothing in it needs a warning. Tag Poetry is the form of the work. The source line leads with the name, carries no em dash and no straight quote, ends the quotation in a full stop, keeps the line breaks with ‘ / ’ and the capitals at the line heads as the 1896 text prints them, and runs 110 characters. Theme fit is strong and is the reason this line is worth saving: we do not know our own height until something asks us to stand up, which is Courage in Trial from the inside, and it is the rare Dickinson that is neither bleak nor arch at six in the morning.

HOW TO FIX IT, NOT KILL IT. Keep the 1896 wording, since the standard allows a line that exists in a named edition and this one does, exactly. Change the source line to the one in betterCitation: first line in place of Todd's title, Life XIV restored, Todd and Roberts Brothers kept, 127 characters, matching the two Dickinson cards already shipped. Then write the note the card is missing, in substance: the title ‘Aspiration’ is Mabel Loomis Todd's, not Dickinson's; the card prints Todd's 1896 text, which reads ‘called to rise’ and, in the stanza not quoted, ‘a daily thing’ where the manuscript text printed since Johnson reads ‘a normal thing’; a reader with a modern Complete Poems will find ‘asked to rise’ in line 2. Say that and the card is honest about what it is, which is the whole of this track's standard. Leave the note empty and the first reader with a Franklin in the house has caught First Light in what looks like a misquotation of the most-quoted poet in the file.
